name: Ipse dixit
statement: A claim is offered with nothing behind it except that somebody asserted it, and the assertion is taken for the reason.
meaning: The Latin means 'he himself said it'. Cicero's Pythagoreans give the strict form: asked why something was so, they answered that the master had said so. Modern use is wider and covers any claim put forward with no stated support, including an expert conclusion with no method behind it. Three neighbouring entries in this atlas take the parts this one leaves out. Argument from authority covers the case where an authority is named and its credentials can be weighed. Authority bias covers behavioural compliance with an instruction. The illusory truth effect covers what repeating an unsupported claim does to belief. What is left here is the narrow question of what an assertion achieves when nothing is offered behind it.

origin.who: John Bowring, editing the papers of Jeremy Bentham
origin.where: Deontology; or, The Science of Morality, volume 1
origin.note: The phrase itself is far older than this date, which is the earliest publication read for this entry that falls inside the range the atlas records. Cicero has it in De Natura Deorum, book 1, section 10, written in the first century BC. Bowring's 'History of the Greatest-Happiness Principle', pages 287 to 332 of the 1834 volume, is where the English derivatives are coined: 'the ipse-dixit root should not produce all the branches necessary to discourse, as ipse-dixitists, and ipse-dixitism' (page 321). The section speaks of Bentham in the third person, so the printed coinage is his editor's.

evidence: The textual record is firm and the measurement record is thin. Cicero's passage is a criticism of deference in argument, and its context is his own preface: 'non enim tam auctoritatis in disputando quam rationis momenta quaerenda sunt', in disputation the weight of reason is to be sought rather than of authority. He then reports what he will not endorse, that the Pythagoreans, asked in debate why a thing was so, used to answer 'ipse dixit', and 'ipse autem erat Pythagoras'. Diogenes Laertius records the Greek form as a proverb at Lives 8.46, where the Perseus text reads that of this Pythagoras 'τὸ Αὐτὸς ἔφα παροιμιακὸν εἰς τὸν βίον ἦλθεν'. Bowring's 1834 gloss traces the term the same way, to 'the principle recognised (so Cicero informs us) by the disciples of Pythagoras', and turns it into the antagonist of the greatest-happiness principle. The phrase entered American evidence law through General Electric Co. v. Joiner, 522 U.S. 136 (1997): nothing in Daubert or the Federal Rules of Evidence 'requires a district court to admit opinion evidence which is connected to existing data only by the ipse dixit of the expert'. That is a rule about what a judge may exclude, not a finding about what listeners believe. The measurement comes from persuasion research, which asks the same question in reverse: what does a message gain by spelling out its support instead of asserting its conclusion? O'Keefe's meta-analysis sorts that literature into three manipulations, argument completeness, information-source citation and quantitative specificity, and codes each comparison as r, positive where the more explicit message won.

replication.headline: No experiment under this name was located. On the nearest measured question, whether spelling out the support for a claim beats asserting it, the pooled advantage is r = 0.138 across 18 experiments on 2,845 people, and the prediction interval for a fresh experiment runs from -0.113 to 0.372.
replication.detail: O'Keefe found 27 argument-completeness cases with 5,808 participants. Pooled, the more explicit message was more persuasive at mean r = .116, 95% CI .052 to .180, with heterogeneity of Q(26) = 75.1, p < .001. The 18 cases that manipulated completeness on its own, N = 2,845, gave mean r = .138, 95% CI .056 to .220. The nine that varied it jointly with another feature gave .078, 95% CI -.016 to .171. Citing the source of the information helped less: 23 cases, N = 5,358, mean r = .064, 95% CI .014 to .114. Quantitative specificity, the contrast between '75%' and 'most', gave 8 cases, N = 2,683, mean r = .060, 95% CI -.020 to .141. On perceived credibility rather than persuasion, the 11 argument-completeness cases pooled to r = .096, 95% CI -.014 to .206. The individual cases in that table run from r = -.285 to r = .465, which is why the verdict here is mixed rather than replicated: the pooled sign is positive and the studies behind it disagree. O'Keefe and Hoeken later recomputed the same two sets inside a survey of 30 message variations covering 1,149 studies and 280,591 participants. Argument explicitness came out at r = 0.138, 95% CI 0.072 to 0.202, with a 95% prediction interval of -0.113 to 0.372; information-source identification at r = 0.072, 95% CI 0.010 to 0.134, prediction interval -0.112 to 0.251. Those are the same effect sizes reanalysed, not new data, and their point is the prediction interval: the median mean r across all 30 variations is about 0.10, and choosing the more explicit message does not reliably win. The other half of the picture is what a bare assertion does on its own. Ye and colleagues pooled 182 illusory-truth studies and 366 effect sizes, N = 31,184, published from 1977 to 2025, and report g = 0.37, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.44 after correcting for small-study effects. Repeating an unsupported statement raises how true it is rated. This atlas covers that literature under the illusory truth effect.

study.cite: O'Keefe, D. J. (1998). Justification explicitness and persuasive effect: A meta-analytic review of the effects of varying support articulation in persuasive messages. Argumentation and Advocacy, 35(2), 61-75.

limits: The persuasion figures are an imperfect proxy and the paper says so. O'Keefe raises the limiting condition himself: two advocates equally explicit about their support may fare differently if one has closely reasoned arguments and the other has shoddy ones, so a pooled estimate over unspecified argument quality cannot say how much a good reason is worth. The cases in his table are old, with dates running from the 1950s to 1997, and heterogeneity is high on every pooled test he reports. The 2021 reanalysis adds prediction intervals rather than participants. On the historical side, the 1824 Book of Fallacies scan held by the Internet Archive was searched in full and contains no occurrence of 'ipse dixit' in any spelling, so the term's Bentham connection rests on the 1834 volume his editor arranged. Whether Bentham used the word in manuscript could not be checked: the Transcribe Bentham page that a search returned would not render, and the Oxford English Dictionary entry recording the word's first use is behind a login. The searches for an experiment carried out under the name covered Crossref, Europe PMC, Google via web search, the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy survey of fallacies, which uses the phrase nowhere in its text, and the reference lists of the two persuasion meta-analyses. None produced one.
misreadings: The commonest error is to treat ipse dixit and the appeal to authority as one thing. Cicero's case is the appeal to authority in its purest form, because the Pythagoreans named their master. Modern usage has drifted away from that: in law and in argument the label now attaches to any conclusion with no support shown, whoever asserts it, and the person asserting is often the one whose credentials nobody disputes. The legal sense is narrower again. Joiner licenses a judge to exclude expert opinion joined to the data only by the expert's say-so, which is a rule about admissibility and carries no claim about whether jurors would have been convinced. The Bentham attribution also gets overstated. The word ipse-dixitism is printed in the 1834 Deontology, in an editorial history written about Bentham rather than by him, and it is used there as the name for every standard of right and wrong other than the greatest-happiness principle rather than as a name for a fallacy of argument. And a small pooled effect for explicitness is not evidence that reasons do not matter: the estimate is an average over messages whose supporting arguments were never rated for quality.
